BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Halloween might be the one night a year when the whole family ends up outside together, moving through the neighborhood in the dark. The post Age-by-age Halloween tips from a board-certified pediatrician first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News.

Actual Article Body:
A new solution in your inbox every day.

BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

Halloween might be the one night a year when the whole family ends up outside together, moving through the neighborhood in the dark. Whether that ends in magic or meltdown depends almost entirely on whether the experience matches the kid you brought with you.

Dr. Kristen Cook, a board-certified pediatrician with more than 15 years of practice in the Midwest, writes that across every age, Halloween offers genuine opportunities to practice life skills like facing fears, managing expectations, developing independence, and showing kindness. How much kids are able to glean out spooky season depends on how you set it up.

The tricky thing about Halloween for little kids is that everything exciting about it is also a lot. Unfamiliar noises, scary decorations, a neighborhood full of costumed kids running in every direction; it can tip from exciting to overwhelming fast.

Dr. Cook’s rule for this age: comfortable over elaborate. Costumes shouldn’t restrict movement or vision, and there’s no reason to push through the full neighborhood circuit after dark. An early start, before it gets busy, tends to go better. Bring a wagon or stroller even if your toddler insists they don’t need one because, let’s face it, they probably will.

Inspect every piece of candy before it’s touched, check for choking hazards and allergens, and agree on a daily candy limit in advance so it’s not a negotiation every time. And if the evening tips into over-stimulation, head home. A short, good Halloween beats a long, tearful one.

Elementary-age kids are ready for more. They can choose their own costumes, help decorate the house, pick out pumpkins, and have real opinions about the trick-or-treating route. Dr. Cook recommends mapping that route together in advance and letting kids take the lead once you’re out.

That said, supervision doesn’t disappear. Pumpkin carving is still an adult activity at this age, and a parent or trusted adult should remain part of the outing, even if they’re hanging back a house or two. Night-friendly costume details matter more here. Think glow bracelets, LED accessories, and reflective elements.

The shift at this stage is toward earned independence. Let them decide who they trick-or-treat with. Let them handle their own candy negotiations. Keep the safety guardrails in place, but make room for them to feel the difference.

By the teenage years, Halloween looks different. Some teens feel too old for trick-or-treating; others still want to be part of it. Dr. Cook’s take is not to push them out of it. Teenagers who help hand out candy, look after younger siblings, or supervise part of the evening have a real role that doesn’t require a costume.

If they’re going out independently, the conversations to have are about curfew, approved locations, and what to do if they end up somewhere uncomfortable. Dr. Cook specifically recommends creating an exit plan before they leave, so they have a way out of an uncomfortable situation without needing to explain themselves in the moment. A standing offer of a no-questions pickup goes a long way.

The bigger ask for teenagers is respect. Taking more than a reasonable amount from an unattended candy bowl, or pulling pranks that leave families upset, isn’t harmless fun. Dr. Cook frames this as a chance to practice the kind of independence that looks like actual maturity.

The memories that stick, Dr. Cook writes, usually aren’t about the costumes or the candy. They’re about the feelings that are attached to them. They remember feeling included, connected, part of something. Halloween doesn’t require expensive gear or elaborate setups. It requires showing up for the kid in front of you, at whatever stage they’re at.

Actual Article Body:

Sign up for email newsletters

Trending:

Halloween candy sales are off to a slow start this year as U.S. consumers grapple with high living costs and eye-popping chocolate prices.

Halloween candy sales fell 6.7% in the month ending Oct. 17 compared to the same period last year, according to NielsenIQ, a market research firm. Nielsen also noted an 11.7% decline in candy sales in mid-September, erasing the preseason gains that Halloween candy enjoyed the previous two years.

Chris Costagli, a vice president and food thought leader at NielsenIQ, said high gas prices have worsened Americans’ concerns about affordability, and that’s dampening demand for Halloween treats. As of Friday, the average price of a gallon of regular gasoline in the U.S. was $4.29, up nearly 40% from the prior year.

“I think what you’re seeing now is a consumer that’s spending so much additional money on fuel and housing and clothing and food,” Costagli said. “Some of the decisions they’re making about Halloween candy, it’s not necessarily because, ‘I notice it’s more expensive than last year,’ it’s, ‘I can’t afford it this year because I’ve paid so much more for so many other things. I just don’t have the financial means to buy it this year.’”

Small bags of candy were the only sizes seeing sales growth through mid-October, Costagli noted. Large and extra-large bags were seeing the biggest declines.

U.S. candy prices have been climbing faster than the rate of inflation for several years. As of September, candy and gum prices were up 44% over a five-year period, according to government data. Prices for all food eaten at home rose 22.5% in the same period.

This week, discount grocer Aldi was advertising a 135-piece variety pack of Mars Inc. chocolate bars – including Milky Way, Trix and Snickers – for $19.87. That’s almost the same price consumers paid for a 250-piece variety pack five years ago.

Cocoa prices are the main culprit. Global cocoa prices reached a record high of $10,710 per metric ton in January 2025 because of poor weather in West Africa – which supplies 70% of the world’s chocolate — and speculative trading in the cocoa futures market, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics.

Cocoa prices had been falling steadily since then, and hit $3,241 per metric ton in March. But they began climbing again in the spring as the Iran war disrupted Africa’s fertilizer supplies. The El Niñoweather pattern is also expected to hurt production, with hot, dry conditions expected through February.

But Costagli noted that even in cases where prices are lower than last year, consumer demand is muted. The average price of non-chocolate Halloween candies, like gummies and lollipops, was $6.08 per pound in the nine weeks ending Oct. 17, which was about 3% lower than last year, according to Nielsen data. But that didn’t lead to a bump in sales.

Sally Lyons Wyatt, a global executive vice president and food industry adviser for the market research company Circana, said one way U.S. consumers have been handling higher grocery pricesis by making smaller and more frequent trips to the supermarket and buying products right before they intend to use them. That makes her wonder if shoppers are waiting until closer to Halloween to buy candy this year.

“People are very intentional and thoughtful about what they want to consume, not just for holidays, but in general,” she said. “I do believe we will still see softness overall with candy, but I don’t think Halloween is doomed.”

The National Confectioners Association, a trade group that represents candy makers like Mars, Smarties Candy Co. and Ferrara Candy Co., said it remains optimistic about Halloween sales.

“We are just now entering the peak period for Halloween and consumer enthusiasm remains incredibly strong,” the group said Friday in a statement.
